description: Hi! I am a young space explorer who loves science, technology and learning about astronauts. I am curious about how astronauts stay healthy and safe while travelling in space. I enjoy solving problems, thinking of creative ideas and learning new things. I want to create health monitoring software that helps astronauts check their health during space missions.
summary:
Astro Health Monitor is an interactive, Scratch-based astronaut health monitoring prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge “Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.”

The project features Commander Nova, a virtual space-health assistant who guides astronauts through daily health check-ups. It collects information through four questions covering heart rate, exercise, sleep, and mood. It also simulates radiation monitoring and random solar storm events to demonstrate potential space-health risks. Based on these inputs, the system evaluates five health systems, displays colour-coded Green, Yellow, or Red alerts, calculates a health score out of 100, and provides personalized health tips and a daily health log.

The project addresses the challenge by demonstrating how regular health monitoring and early warning alerts can help astronauts become more aware of potential health risks during space missions. It is important because space conditions such as microgravity, radiation, isolation, and disrupted sleep can affect astronauts' physical and mental well-being. By making health monitoring interactive and easy to understand, Astro Health Monitor promotes preventive healthcare awareness and encourages safer, healthier space exploration.
details:
ASTRO HEALTH MONITOR

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Project Name: Astro Health Monitor
Project Concept: Daily Space Health Check-ups with Commander Nova
Team Name: ORBIT HEALTH SQUAD
Platform: Scratch 3.0
Selected Challenge: Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
Theme: The Next Frontier

1. Introduction - Understanding the Problem

Space exploration is one of humanity's greatest technological achievements. However, sending astronauts into space creates several challenges that can affect their physical and mental health.

Unlike people living on Earth, astronauts work in an environment where gravity is extremely low, radiation exposure can be higher, normal day-and-night cycles are disrupted, and long periods of isolation can affect their emotional well-being.

Some of the major health challenges faced by astronauts include:

a. Microgravity and bone loss

In space, astronauts do not experience the same gravitational force that keeps their bones and muscles active on Earth. Over time, this can lead to reduced bone density and muscle strength. Regular exercise is therefore an important part of maintaining astronaut health.

b. Changes in heart rate and body fluids

Microgravity causes body fluids to shift towards the upper body and head. This can influence the cardiovascular system and create changes in how the body functions.

c. Sleep disturbances

Astronauts can experience approximately 16 sunrises and sunsets every 24 hours while orbiting Earth. This unusual light cycle can disturb their natural sleep patterns and affect their recovery.

d. Mental and emotional health

Astronauts spend extended periods away from family, friends, and familiar surroundings. Isolation, workload, and unusual living conditions can affect their mood and emotional well-being.

e. Space radiation and solar storms

Astronauts are exposed to radiation from space. Solar storms can increase radiation exposure and potentially damage cells and DNA.

The problem we are addressing

Astronauts need to monitor several health indicators regularly. However, identifying warning signs early and understanding how different space conditions affect their health can be challenging.

Our central question was:

How can we make daily astronaut health monitoring simple, interactive, and understandable so that potential health concerns can be identified early?

To address this challenge, we developed Astro Health Monitor, an interactive health-monitoring prototype using Scratch 3.0.

2. Our Proposed Solution – Astro Health Monitor

Astro Health Monitor is an interactive astronaut health-monitoring dashboard in which a virtual space assistant named Commander Nova guides the astronaut through a daily health check-up.

Instead of presenting the astronaut with complicated medical information, the system asks simple questions about important health parameters, simulates radiation monitoring, evaluates the collected information, and provides understandable feedback.

The project combines:

  • Interactive user input.
  • Daily health check-ups.
  • Heart-rate monitoring through user-provided information.
  • Exercise and physical activity tracking.
  • Sleep-duration monitoring.
  • Mood and emotional well-being assessment.
  • Simulated space-radiation monitoring.
  • Random solar storm events.
  • Five colour-coded health indicators.
  • An overall health score out of 100.
  • Health recommendations and a daily health log.
  • An educational quiz with a score out of 4.

The main innovation is the use of a friendly virtual space-health assistant to turn a health-monitoring process into an interactive learning experience.

3. Step-by-Step Working of the Project

Step 1: Starting the Astro Health Monitor

When the user opens the Scratch project, the astronaut health-monitoring interface appears.

The user is introduced to Commander Nova, who acts as the virtual health assistant throughout the experience.

The user can start the process by clicking the CHECK-UP button.

This button initiates the daily health assessment.

Once the check-up begins, Commander Nova guides the user through a sequence of questions and monitoring activities.

Purpose: To create a simple and friendly starting point that allows an astronaut to begin a daily health assessment without navigating complicated menus.

Step 2: Commander Nova Collects the Astronaut's Health Information

After the user clicks CHECK-UP, Commander Nova begins asking four questions.

These questions are designed to collect information about four important aspects of astronaut health:

  1. Heart rate.
  2. Exercise duration.
  3. Sleep duration.
  4. Mood and emotional well-being.

The user provides answers to each question, and the system uses those responses as inputs for the health assessment.

Parameter 1: Heart Rate Monitoring

Question asked: What is your current heart rate?

Heart rate refers to the number of times the heart beats in one minute. It is measured in beats per minute (BPM).

Heart rate is an important indicator of cardiovascular activity. Monitoring it helps an astronaut become aware of changes in their body's physical condition.

Reference range used in our prototype:

  • 60–100 BPM: Reference healthy range.
  • Below or above this range: Requires attention in the prototype's assessment.

How it works in our project:

  1. Commander Nova asks the user to enter their current heart rate.
  2. The user provides a numerical value.
  3. The system compares the entered value with the reference range.
  4. The heart-rate indicator is evaluated.
  5. The system uses the result while preparing the overall health assessment.

Why this parameter is important:

Changes in heart rate can provide useful information about cardiovascular activity. Regular monitoring can help astronauts become more aware of their physical condition during space missions.

Note: The heart rate in this prototype is entered by the user. It is not measured using a connected heart-rate sensor.

Parameter 2: Exercise and Bone Health Monitoring

Question asked: How much time did you exercise today?

Exercise is especially important for astronauts because microgravity reduces the normal loading forces experienced by bones and muscles.

Without regular physical activity, astronauts can experience muscle weakening and loss of bone density.

Our project uses the concept of approximately two hours of daily exercise as a space-health reference.

How it works in our project:

  1. Commander Nova asks the astronaut how much time they exercised.
  2. The user enters or selects the duration of their exercise.
  3. The system evaluates the reported exercise duration against the daily exercise reference.
  4. The exercise-related health indicator reflects whether the astronaut is meeting the expected activity target.
  5. The result contributes to the overall health assessment.

Why this parameter is important:

Regular exercise helps astronauts maintain muscle strength, support bone health, and reduce some of the physical effects associated with microgravity.

This parameter encourages astronauts to develop a consistent exercise routine instead of neglecting physical activity during space missions.

Parameter 3: Sleep Monitoring

Question asked: How many hours did you sleep today?

Sleep is essential for physical recovery, concentration, memory, and emotional stability.

Astronauts may experience sleep disturbances because of unusual light cycles, mission schedules, and the environment inside a spacecraft.

Our prototype uses 7–8 hours of sleep as its reference range.

How it works in our project:

  1. Commander Nova asks the astronaut how many hours they slept.
  2. The user enters the number of hours.
  3. The system compares the reported duration with the reference range.
  4. The sleep-related health indicator is evaluated.
  5. The system considers the result when preparing the overall health score and recommendations.

Why this parameter is important:

Insufficient sleep can affect concentration, decision-making, mood, and physical recovery.

By including sleep monitoring, our project highlights the importance of maintaining a healthy sleeping routine during long-duration space missions.

Parameter 4: Mood and Emotional Well-being Monitoring

Question asked: How is your mood today?

Physical health is not the only factor that determines an astronaut's well-being. Mental and emotional health are equally important.

Astronauts can experience stress, loneliness, isolation, and emotional difficulties during extended missions.

To make mood assessment simple, our project uses a numerical rating system from 1 to 5.

The user selects a number representing their current mood:

How it works in our project:

  1. Commander Nova asks the astronaut how they are feeling.
  2. The user selects a mood rating from 1 to 5.
  3. The system receives the selected rating.
  4. The emotional well-being indicator reflects the reported mood.
  5. The result is considered in the overall health assessment.

Why this parameter is important:

An astronaut might have a normal heart rate and sufficient sleep but still experience emotional stress.

By including mood assessment, we acknowledge that astronaut health must include both physical and psychological well-being.

This feature also encourages astronauts to pay attention to their emotional condition and recognise when they may need support.

4. Automated Space Radiation Monitoring

One of the most important features of Astro Health Monitor is its simulated radiation-monitoring mechanism.

Unlike the four health parameters, which are collected through user responses, radiation is evaluated automatically within the Scratch project using randomly generated values.

This feature demonstrates how an automated monitoring system can continuously check environmental conditions and generate alerts when radiation levels increase.

Understanding Space Radiation

Space radiation consists of energetic particles and radiation originating from sources such as the Sun and outside our solar system.

During solar events, including solar storms, radiation exposure can increase.

This creates a potential risk to astronauts, particularly during long-duration missions.

Our project demonstrates this challenge through a simulated radiation sensor.

How the Random Radiation Calculation Works

The radiation-monitoring mechanism uses two different ranges of randomly generated values.

A. Normal radiation simulation

When a normal monitoring condition is used, the Scratch project generates a random radiation value between:

0.4 mSv and 1.6 mSv

The generated value represents the simulated radiation reading.

The prototype uses the following reference:

  • Below 1.3 mSv: Within the project's reference threshold.
  • Above 1.3 mSv: Requires attention and may trigger a warning.

B. Solar storm simulation

To demonstrate the effect of a solar storm, the project generates a higher radiation value within the range:

2.1 mSv to 4.0 mSv

These higher values represent a simulated increase in radiation exposure during a solar event.

The system can then generate a radiation-related health alert.

Step-by-Step Automated Radiation Workflow

  1. After the astronaut completes the four health questions, the radiation-monitoring process is initiated.
  2. The Scratch program generates a random numerical value within the normal radiation range.
  3. The system evaluates the generated value against the reference threshold of 1.3 mSv.
  4. A simulated solar storm event can trigger a second, higher radiation range.
  5. When the solar storm condition is activated, a random value between 2.1 and 4.0 mSv is generated.
  6. The system identifies that the simulated radiation exposure has increased.
  7. A radiation warning is displayed through the health-monitoring interface.
  8. The radiation result contributes to the overall health assessment.

Example of how the radiation simulation works

These are illustrative examples of possible generated readings, not actual measurements from space.

Why did we use random number generation?

Random number generation makes the simulation dynamic.

If the system always displayed the same radiation reading, the user would not experience different environmental conditions.

By introducing random values, we can demonstrate different situations:

  • Normal radiation conditions.
  • Increased radiation levels.
  • Simulated solar storm events.
  • Radiation-related warning conditions.

This makes the project more engaging and demonstrates the concept of automated environmental monitoring.

Important technical clarification: The radiation sensor in our current Scratch prototype is simulated using random number generation. It is not connected to a physical radiation detector, and the generated values do not represent actual astronaut exposure. The project's numerical thresholds are demonstration references rather than validated medical or mission-safety limits.

5. Five Health Indicators and Colour-Coded Monitoring

After collecting the astronaut's responses and completing the radiation simulation, the project presents the results through five health indicators.

These indicators make the health assessment easier to understand.

Instead of displaying only numerical values, the project uses three colours to communicate the status of the monitored parameters.

Green – Healthy / Normal

Green indicates that the evaluated parameter is within the project's defined reference condition.

Yellow – Warning / Attention Required

Yellow indicates that a parameter requires attention or that the astronaut should consider improving a particular health habit.

Red – Critical / Alert

Red indicates a more concerning condition in the prototype and highlights the need for immediate attention within the simulation.

The five monitored dimensions are represented by:

  1. Heart-rate status.
  2. Exercise and bone-health status.
  3. Sleep status.
  4. Mood and emotional well-being status.
  5. Radiation exposure status.

Why colour-coded indicators?

Colour coding helps users understand the results quickly.

For example, an astronaut does not need to interpret several complicated numerical values to recognise that a parameter requires attention.

The indicators make the dashboard easier to understand and help users identify which areas of their health need improvement.

6. Overall Health Score - Score Out of 100

After evaluating the five health indicators, Astro Health Monitor presents an overall health score out of 100.

The purpose of this score is to provide a simple overview of the astronaut's daily health assessment.

The score brings together the results from:

  • Heart rate.
  • Exercise.
  • Sleep.
  • Mood.
  • Radiation monitoring.

For example, an astronaut who reports sufficient sleep, regular exercise, a reference-range heart rate, and a positive mood, while receiving a normal simulated radiation reading, would generally receive a more favourable assessment than someone whose inputs indicate several areas requiring attention.

The health score makes the results easier to interpret and allows the user to understand their overall assessment at a glance.

Why is the health score important?

  • It summarises multiple health indicators in one place.
  • It helps users identify areas that need improvement.
  • It makes daily health monitoring more interactive.
  • It encourages users to pay attention to their daily health habits.

The score is an educational prototype score, not a clinically validated measure of astronaut health.

7. Personalised Health Tips and Recommendations

After calculating the overall health assessment, Commander Nova provides simple health recommendations based on the monitored parameters.

The purpose is not simply to tell the astronaut whether a parameter is healthy or unhealthy, but also to explain what they can do to improve their daily routine.

Examples of relevant recommendations include:

Heart rate: Pay attention to your heart-rate reading and seek appropriate medical guidance if it is outside the expected range.

Exercise: Maintain a regular exercise routine to support bone and muscle health.

Sleep: Follow a consistent sleep schedule and aim for the project's 7–8-hour reference.

Mood: Pay attention to emotional well-being, maintain communication with your support network, and seek support when needed.

Radiation: Monitor radiation alerts and follow the appropriate mission safety procedures when exposure increases.

These recommendations connect the assessment results with practical health-awareness messages.

8. Daily Health Log

Another important feature is the Health Log.

The purpose of the log is to maintain a record of the astronaut's daily check-up information.

A health log can help users review the information collected during their assessment, including their health inputs, monitoring results, and overall score.

This concept is particularly important for long-duration space missions because health monitoring should not be treated as a one-time activity.

Maintaining daily records can help astronauts and their support teams understand changes over time and identify patterns that may require further investigation.

The log feature also demonstrates how software can organise health information in a structured manner.

9. Interactive Educational Quiz

Along with monitoring astronaut health, Astro Health Monitor includes an educational quiz.

The quiz is designed to reinforce the knowledge gained during the health check-up.

It helps users understand why different health parameters matter and how the space environment affects the human body.

The quiz is scored out of 4 points.

Each question contributes to the user's learning assessment, with the total score indicating how well they understood the concepts presented in the project.

Purpose of the quiz

The quiz reinforces important learning areas, including:

  • Why astronauts need regular exercise.
  • How microgravity affects bones and muscles.
  • Why sleep is important during space missions.
  • Why astronauts need to monitor their mood.
  • How space radiation and solar storms can affect astronaut safety.

The quiz turns the project into more than a monitoring dashboard. It also becomes an interactive educational experience.

It encourages users to think about the science behind astronaut health rather than simply clicking through the interface.

The presentation confirms a four-point quiz but does not list its exact question wording, answer options, or answer-validation logic. Those details should be added from the actual Scratch quiz scripts rather than assumed.

10. Complete User Journey - From Start to Finish

The following sequence explains the complete experience of using Astro Health Monitor.

Stage 1 – Project Launch

The user opens the Scratch project and enters the astronaut health-monitoring interface.

Stage 2 – Commander Nova Introduction

Commander Nova welcomes the user and introduces the daily health check-up.

Stage 3 – Start Check-up

The user clicks the CHECK-UP button to begin the process.

Stage 4 – Heart Rate Input

Commander Nova asks for the astronaut's heart rate. The user enters the BPM value.

Stage 5 – Exercise Input

The system asks how much time the astronaut exercised. The user provides the exercise duration.

Stage 6 – Sleep Input

The user enters the number of hours they slept.

Stage 7 – Mood Assessment

The user selects a mood rating from 1 to 5, ranging from sad to very good.

Stage 8 – Automated Radiation Simulation

The Scratch program generates a random radiation reading. A simulated solar storm can introduce a higher radiation value and trigger an alert.

Stage 9 – Health Status Evaluation

The system evaluates the five health dimensions and presents Green, Yellow, or Red indicators.

Stage 10 – Health Score

The system displays an overall health score out of 100.

Stage 11 – Health Recommendations

Commander Nova provides health-related tips to encourage better daily habits and awareness.

Stage 12 – Health Log

The check-up information is presented as a health-log entry.

Stage 13 – Educational Quiz

The user participates in a four-point quiz to reinforce their understanding of astronaut health and space-related risks.

Stage 14 – Learning and Awareness

The user completes the experience with a better understanding of how space conditions can affect astronaut health and why continuous monitoring matters.

11. Challenges Addressed and Solutions Developed

Our project focuses on five major challenges associated with astronaut health.

Challenge 1: Difficulty monitoring multiple health parameters

Problem: Astronaut health depends on several factors, and focusing on only one measurement may not provide a complete picture.

Our solution: We combined four user-provided health parameters with automated radiation simulation to create a unified daily health assessment.

Challenge 2: Identifying possible warning signs

Problem: Health-related changes may go unnoticed if information is not reviewed regularly.

Our solution: We introduced five colour-coded health indicators and an overall health score to make the results easier to interpret.

Challenge 3: Monitoring environmental radiation risks

Problem: Radiation exposure can increase during solar events and may create additional risks for astronauts.

Our solution: We developed a simulated radiation-monitoring mechanism using random number generation and higher readings during simulated solar storm conditions.

Challenge 4: Addressing mental health

Problem: Physical health measurements alone cannot represent an astronaut's complete well-being.

Our solution: We included a mood assessment so that emotional well-being becomes part of the daily health check-up.

Challenge 5: Making health information easy to understand

Problem: Health and space-science information can be complicated, particularly for people who are not familiar with the subject.

Our solution: We introduced Commander Nova, colour-coded feedback, simple health recommendations, and an educational quiz to make the experience interactive and accessible.

12. Innovation and Uniqueness of Our Project

The key innovation of Astro Health Monitor is the combination of health awareness, environmental-risk simulation, and interactive learning in one Scratch-based prototype.

Our project introduces several important ideas:

1. Virtual Space Health Assistant

Commander Nova acts as a friendly guide who makes the health-monitoring process easier to follow.

2. Combination of Manual and Automated Monitoring

The project combines information entered by the astronaut with automatically generated radiation readings.

3. Solar Storm Simulation

Random number generation allows the project to demonstrate how radiation conditions can change and how the system can respond to higher simulated readings.

4. Physical and Emotional Health Together

The project recognises that astronaut health includes cardiovascular activity, exercise, sleep, and emotional well-being, in addition to environmental exposure.

5. Visual Health Dashboard

The five colour-coded indicators and overall score provide an accessible way to understand the assessment.

6. Learning Through Interaction

The educational quiz reinforces the scientific concepts behind astronaut health monitoring.

13. Technologies and Tools Used

Scratch 3.0

We developed the prototype using Scratch 3.0, a block-based programming environment.

Scratch allows us to build interactive projects using sprites, scripts, variables, conditions, operators, broadcasts, and events.

The project uses the programming concepts needed to create an interactive user experience.

The project demonstrates how block-based programming can be used to build an interactive simulation of a real-world technological challenge.

14. Expected Impact and Future Scope

Astro Health Monitor is intended to demonstrate how a simple software interface can make astronaut health monitoring more understandable and accessible.

Its expected educational and conceptual benefits include:

  • Increasing awareness of the health challenges associated with space exploration.
  • Encouraging regular monitoring of important health parameters.
  • Demonstrating the importance of exercise and sleep in microgravity.
  • Highlighting the relationship between emotional well-being and mission performance.
  • Introducing the concept of radiation monitoring and solar storm alerts.
  • Demonstrating how automated alerts and data visualisation can support health-awareness systems.

Future Improvements

The current project is a Scratch-based prototype. It can be developed further into a more advanced astronaut health-monitoring platform.

Possible improvements include:

1. Real sensor integration

Connect compatible heart-rate monitoring hardware and other suitable health sensors to collect real measurements rather than relying on manual input.

2. Actual radiation sensor integration

Explore integration with appropriate radiation-detection hardware to replace the simulated random readings with measured data.

3. Historical health analytics

Develop a system that stores daily health records and displays trends over time.

4. Improved alert mechanisms

Introduce more detailed warning levels and notification mechanisms for different health conditions.

5. Advanced health analytics

Explore data analysis techniques to identify unusual patterns and support earlier review by qualified medical professionals.

6. Communication with medical support teams

Explore how astronaut health information could be securely shared with authorised medical teams on Earth.

These are future development possibilities and are not claimed as existing capabilities of the current Scratch prototype.

15. Conclusion

Astro Health Monitor demonstrates how an interactive software solution can help communicate the importance of astronaut health monitoring during space missions.

Through Commander Nova, astronauts are guided through a daily health check-up that evaluates heart rate, exercise, sleep, and mood. The project also introduces simulated radiation monitoring and solar storm events using random number generation.

The five colour-coded indicators, overall health score, personalised health tips, health log, and educational quiz combine to create an engaging health-awareness experience.

Our project addresses an important challenge in space exploration: understanding and monitoring the different factors that can affect astronaut well-being during long-duration missions.

Although this prototype does not replace professional medical systems or actual space radiation detectors, it demonstrates a foundation for exploring how software, automation, data monitoring, and interactive interfaces can contribute to future astronaut health-support solutions.

Our vision is simple: astronauts explore the next frontier, and technology helps them take care of their health along the way.
